---
title: Improve hypertable and query performance
description: Use chunk skipping to optimize hypertable performance and make sure your analytical queries are as fast as they can be
---

import * as C from "@constants";
import { Callout } from "@stainless-api/docs/components";
import { NumberedList, NumberedItem } from "@components/NumberedList";

import ChunkInterval from "../../../../partials/_chunk-interval.mdx";
import EarlyAccess2171 from "../../../../partials/_early_access_2_17_1.mdx";

{C.HYPERTABLE_CAP}s are {C.PG} tables that help you improve insert and query performance by automatically partitioning
your data by time. Each {C.HYPERTABLE} is made up of child tables called {C.CHUNK}s. Each {C.CHUNK} is assigned a range of time,
and only contains data from that range. When you run a query, {C.TIMESCALE_DB} identifies the correct {C.CHUNK} and runs
the query on it, instead of going through the entire table. This page shows you how to tune {C.HYPERTABLE}s to increase
performance even more.

- [Optimize {C.HYPERTABLE} {C.CHUNK} intervals](#optimize-hypertable-chunk-intervals): choose the optimum {C.CHUNK} size for your data
- [Enable {C.CHUNK_SKIPPING}](#enable-chunk-skipping): skip {C.CHUNK}s on non-partitioning columns in {C.HYPERTABLE}s when you query your data
- [Analyze your {C.HYPERTABLE}s](#analyze-your-hypertables): use {C.PG} `ANALYZE` to create the best query plan

## Optimize {C.HYPERTABLE} {C.CHUNK} intervals

Adjusting your {C.HYPERTABLE} {C.CHUNK} interval can improve performance in your database.

<NumberedList>

  <NumberedItem title={`Choose an optimum ${C.CHUNK} interval`}>

    <ChunkInterval />

    In the following example you create a table called `conditions` that stores time values in the
    `time` column and has {C.CHUNK}s that store data for a `chunk_interval` of one day:

    ```sql
    CREATE TABLE conditions (
       time        TIMESTAMPTZ       NOT NULL,
       location    TEXT              NOT NULL,
       device      TEXT              NOT NULL,
       temperature DOUBLE PRECISION  NULL,
       humidity    DOUBLE PRECISION  NULL
    ) WITH (
       tsdb.hypertable,
       tsdb.chunk_interval='1 day'
    );
    ```

  </NumberedItem>

  <NumberedItem title={`Check current setting for ${C.CHUNK} intervals`}>

    Query the {C.TIMESCALE_DB} catalog for a {C.HYPERTABLE}. For example:

    ```sql
    SELECT *
      FROM timescaledb_information.dimensions
      WHERE hypertable_name = 'conditions';
    ```

    The result looks like:

    ```sql
    hypertable_schema | hypertable_name | dimension_number | column_name |       column_type        | dimension_type | time_interval | integer_interval | integer_now_func | num_partitions
    -------------------+-----------------+------------------+-------------+--------------------------+----------------+---------------+------------------+------------------+----------------
     public           | metrics          |                1 | recorded    | timestamp with time zone | Time           | 1 day         |                  |                  |
    ```

    Time-based interval lengths are reported in microseconds.

  </NumberedItem>

  <NumberedItem title={`Change the ${C.CHUNK} interval length on an existing ${C.HYPERTABLE}`}>

    To change the {C.CHUNK} interval on an already existing {C.HYPERTABLE}, call
    [`set_chunk_time_interval()`](/api-reference/timescaledb/hypertables/set_chunk_time_interval).

    ```sql
    SELECT set_chunk_time_interval('conditions', INTERVAL '24 hours');
    ```

    The updated {C.CHUNK} interval only applies to new {C.CHUNK}s. This means setting an overly long
    interval might take a long time to correct. For example, if you set
    `chunk_interval` to 1 year and start inserting data, you can no longer
    shorten the {C.CHUNK} for that year. If you need to correct this situation, create a
    new {C.HYPERTABLE} and migrate your data.

    While {C.CHUNK} turnover does not degrade performance, {C.CHUNK} creation
    does take longer lock time than a normal `INSERT` operation into a {C.CHUNK} that has
    already been created. This means that if multiple {C.CHUNK}s are being created at
    the same time, the transactions block each other until the first transaction is
    completed.

  </NumberedItem>

</NumberedList>

If you use expensive index types, such as some PostGIS geospatial indexes, take
care to check the total size of the {C.CHUNK} and its index using
[`chunks_detailed_size()`](/api-reference/timescaledb/hypertables/chunks_detailed_size).

## Enable {C.CHUNK_SKIPPING}

<EarlyAccess2171 />

One of the key purposes of {C.HYPERTABLE}s is to make your analytical queries run with the lowest latency possible.
When you execute a query on a {C.HYPERTABLE}, you do not parse the whole table; you only access the {C.CHUNK}s necessary
to satisfy the query. This works well when the `WHERE` clause of a query uses the column by which a {C.HYPERTABLE} is
partitioned. For example, in a {C.HYPERTABLE} where every day of the year is a separate {C.CHUNK}, a query for September 1
accesses only the {C.CHUNK} for that day.

However, many queries use columns other than the partitioning one. For example, a satellite company might have a
table with two columns: one for when data was gathered by a satellite and one for when it was added to the database.
If you partition by the date of gathering, a query by the date of adding accesses all {C.CHUNK}s in the {C.HYPERTABLE} and
slows the performance.

To improve query performance, {C.TIMESCALE_DB} enables you to skip {C.CHUNK}s on non-partitioning columns in {C.HYPERTABLE}s.

<Callout variant="warning">
{C.CHUNK_SKIPPING_CAP} only works on {C.CHUNK}s converted to the {C.COLUMNSTORE} **after** you `enable_chunk_skipping`.
</Callout>

### How {C.CHUNK_SKIPPING} works

You enable {C.CHUNK_SKIPPING} on a column in a {C.HYPERTABLE}. {C.TIMESCALE_DB} tracks the minimum and maximum values for that
column in each {C.CHUNK}. These ranges are stored in the start (inclusive) and end (exclusive) format in the `chunk_column_stats`
catalog table. {C.TIMESCALE_DB} uses these ranges for dynamic {C.CHUNK} exclusion when the `WHERE` clause of an SQL query
specifies ranges on the column.

![Chunk skipping](https://assets.timescale.com/docs/images/hypertable-with-chunk-skipping.png)

You can enable {C.CHUNK_SKIPPING} on {C.HYPERTABLE}s compressed into the {C.COLUMNSTORE} for `smallint`, `int`, `bigint`, `serial`,
`bigserial`, `date`, `timestamp`, or `timestamptz` type columns.

### When to enable {C.CHUNK_SKIPPING}

You can enable {C.CHUNK_SKIPPING} on as many columns as you need. However, best practice is to enable it on columns that
are both:

- Correlated, that is, related to the partitioning column in some way.
- Referenced in the `WHERE` clauses of the queries.

In the satellite example, the time of adding data to a database inevitably follows the time of gathering.
Sequential IDs and the creation timestamp for both entities also increase synchronously. This means those two
columns are correlated.

For a more in-depth look on {C.CHUNK_SKIPPING}, see [our blog post](https://www.tigerdata.com/blog/boost-postgres-performance-by-7x-with-chunk-skipping-indexes).

### Enable {C.CHUNK_SKIPPING}

To enable {C.CHUNK_SKIPPING} on a column, call [`enable_chunk_skipping()`](/api-reference/timescaledb/hypertables/enable_chunk_skipping)
on a {C.HYPERTABLE} for a `column_name`. For example, the following query enables {C.CHUNK_SKIPPING} on the `order_id` column
in the `orders` table:

```sql
SELECT enable_chunk_skipping('orders', 'order_id');
```

For more details on how to implement {C.CHUNK_SKIPPING}, see the [API reference](/api-reference/timescaledb/hypertables/enable_chunk_skipping).

## Analyze your {C.HYPERTABLE}s

You can use the {C.PG} `ANALYZE` command to query all {C.CHUNK}s in your
{C.HYPERTABLE}. The statistics collected by the `ANALYZE` command are used by the
{C.PG} planner to create the best query plan. For more information about the
`ANALYZE` command, see the [{C.PG} documentation](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/sql-analyze.html).
